title: India's balance sheet: who saves, who borrows, and who fills the gap
hook:
In the summer of 2013 India's finance minister, P. Chidambaram, did something few finance ministers ever do. He asked his fellow citizens, more or less directly, to stop buying gold. If you were going to buy twenty grams, he suggested, could you buy ten? He raised import duties, told banks not to push gold on customers, and the RBI asked banks to stop selling gold coins.

Why would a finance minister lecture a nation about wedding jewellery? Because gold is imported, it is paid for in dollars, and in 2013 India did not have enough dollars. The country was investing far more than it was saving, the gap was being filled by fickle foreign money, and that money was leaving. Gold was simply the easiest item on the bill to point at.

That episode captures this chapter in one scene. Every macro crisis India has had shows up first on the national balance sheet: who saves, who borrows, and how much has to be borrowed from abroad. Understand those three, and you will know why an oil shock is a nuisance one year and a crisis the next.
short: Investment equals domestic saving plus foreign saving. Whatever India invests beyond what it saves has to be borrowed from the world, and that gap is the current account deficit.
Households are the country's big savers, but their net financial surplus has thinned because borrowing for homes, cars and consumption grew faster than their savings.
The government takes the first and largest claim on those savings, through rules that make banks, insurers and pension funds hold its bonds.
The external gap now leans more on portfolio money, including passive bond-index money, and less on sticky direct investment. That is why an oil shock bites harder than the headline deficit suggests.

sections.heading: The one identity every Indian macro story obeys
sections.html:
Start with the only equation in this chapter, and it is accounting, not theory. A country's investment, meaning the new factories, roads, homes and machines it builds in a year, has to be paid for by somebody's savings. Either the country saves enough itself, or it borrows the difference from the rest of the world.

Think of a family building a house. They can pay from their own savings, or borrow from relatives in the Gulf. If the house costs more than they have saved, the shortfall is, by definition, what they borrowed. India works the same way. When India invests more than it saves, the shortfall shows up as the current account deficit: the gap between what India pays the world for goods, services and interest, and what it earns from the world.

So the current account deficit is not just a trade statistic. It is the amount of foreign savings India is using. That reframing is worth holding on to, because it tells you where to look when the deficit widens. Either investment is booming, which is healthy, or domestic saving has fallen, or something like oil has made the import bill jump.

[[fig:1]]

The diagram traces the plumbing from left to right. Households save, into deposits, funds, insurance, gold and property. Banks, funds and insurers pool that money and pass it on. Then come the claims on the pool: the government gets first call, then companies and households who want to borrow. Whatever is left unfunded at the far right is the external gap, filled by foreign direct investment, portfolio flows, foreign loans and deposits from Indians abroad. Most Indian macro stress shows up at the boundary between the last two boxes.

sections.heading: Indian households: big savers, thinner cushion
sections.html:
In India's balance sheet, households are the lender of the nation. Companies borrow to build, the government borrows to spend, and households, with their fixed deposits, provident funds, insurance policies and gold, supply most of the money.

Here's the distinction that matters: gross financial saving versus net financial saving. Gross is everything households put into financial assets. Net is that minus what they borrowed in the same year. A family that puts money into a SIP while taking a home loan and buying a phone on instalments may be saving plenty in gross terms and very little in net terms.

After the pandemic, that is roughly what happened across the country. Gross saving into financial assets stayed healthy. But borrowing jumped: home loans, car loans, personal loans, credit cards and the buy-now-pay-later schemes that make a television feel affordable. The net financial surplus of households fell to its lowest level in roughly five decades.

Does that mean Indian households are in trouble? Not necessarily, and the debate is genuinely two-sided. Part of the borrowing built houses, which is saving in physical form rather than financial form. Part was a release of the precautionary cash people had hoarded during lockdowns. But the arithmetic of the identity does not care about motives. A thinner household surplus means less domestic money is left over to fund the government and companies, so more of India's investment has to be funded from abroad.

Households are still saving. They are also borrowing more, and the nation only gets to use the difference.

For investors, this cuts two ways. Lenders that grew fast on unsecured consumer credit carry the risk if incomes stall. And the cushion behind domestic equity flows, the buffer the prologue described, is thinner than the headline SIP numbers suggest.

sections.heading: From fixed deposits to SIPs: where the savings now go
sections.html:
For decades the Indian household portfolio had three pillars: bank deposits, gold and property. Shares were for a small, mostly urban minority, and many of them had been burned in a scam or two.

That changed over the past decade. The provident fund began putting a slice of contributions into index funds in 2015. SIPs became the default way for salaried Indians to invest. The pandemic brought millions of first-time investors into the market. Insurance-linked products and the National Pension System added more steady money. The result is a big shift in composition: a far larger share of household saving now reaches the stock market every month, automatically, from salary accounts.

That shift is the reason domestic institutions can now absorb heavy foreign selling. When foreign funds sell, Indian mutual funds have fresh SIP money to deploy, and insurers have premiums to invest. It is a structural buyer that did not exist at this scale in 2013.

But households never left their old loves.

[[fig:2]]

The chart puts the two big financial choices side by side, both indexed to the same starting point in mid-2015. Look at how far gold in rupees has outrun the Nifty over the decade, with most of the gap opening up in the stress years. The reason is in the caption: gold priced in rupees benefits twice in a crisis, once because the dollar gold price rises when the world gets scared, and again because the rupee weakens. For a household, gold is a hedge against exactly the shocks this course is about. That is why the jewellery counter stays busy even in a bull market, and why gold imports keep showing up on India's external bill.

sections.heading: The government's first claim
sections.html:
Now the biggest borrower. The government spends more than it collects in taxes, and the gap, the fiscal deficit, is borrowed by selling bonds. Add the centre and the states together and they absorb a large share of the country's financial savings every year.

The government does not have to compete very hard for that money, and this is the key point. Indian rules make sure there are natural buyers. Banks must hold a minimum slice of their deposits in government bonds, a requirement called the statutory liquidity ratio. Insurers and pension funds, which owe money decades into the future, need long-dated safe bonds and are steered towards government paper. The provident fund holds large amounts too. So a big portion of your deposit, your insurance premium and your provident fund contribution ends up, one way or another, funding the government.

That is why the government's claim is described as first and sticky. It gets funded before anyone else, and it does not shrink quickly. One quiet change of recent years is the states. State government borrowing now rivals the centre's in size, and it gets far less attention, even though every state bond competes for the same pool of savings.

What does it mean for markets? When the government borrows heavily, there is less left for companies, and the price of money rises for everyone. Economists call this crowding out. You see it in bond yields: when government borrowing rises faster than household saving, yields drift up, and so does the cost of a corporate loan. You also see it in banks: lenders with a big chunk of their balance sheet in government bonds take a hit when yields rise, because the market value of those bonds falls.

sections.heading: The external gap, and who fills it
sections.html:
What's left over after households, the government and companies have settled up is the external gap. On the spending side, the big items are crude oil, gold, electronics and coal. On the earning side, India has two great strengths: its software and business services exports, and the money Indians working abroad send home, among the largest in the world.

The gap gets funded in four main ways, and the mix matters more than the total.

  • Foreign direct investment: a foreign company building a factory or buying a controlling stake. It is sticky; nobody dismantles a plant because of a bad week.
  • Portfolio flows: foreign funds buying Indian shares and bonds. Fast in, fast out.
  • Foreign loans: Indian companies borrowing abroad in dollars, which leaves them exposed if the rupee falls.
  • Deposits from Indians abroad: steady in normal times, and a tool the RBI has used in emergencies.

Here's the worrying part. Net direct investment has weakened. Gross money still comes in, but more goes back out: foreign parents selling stakes in their Indian arms, private equity funds cashing out through share sales and Indian companies investing abroad. So the gap leans more on portfolio money.

Part of that portfolio money is a new kind. Since 2024, Indian government bonds have been included in global bond indices. Funds that track those indices must hold Indian bonds in proportion to the index weight, whatever they think of India. That brought in steady money and helped keep bond yields lower. But it also means a decision taken by an index committee abroad, or a fund redemption wave in New York, now flows straight into the rupee.

sections.heading: Why stress always shows up at the boundary
sections.html:
Put the pieces together and you can see how an Indian macro crisis unfolds, step by step.

It starts with a shock to the external gap, usually oil. The import bill jumps, so the gap widens. If that gap is funded by sticky direct investment, little happens. But if it is funded by portfolio money, the same shock that widens the gap often makes that money nervous, and it leaves at exactly the moment it is most needed. The rupee weakens.

Then the RBI steps in and sells dollars from its reserves to slow the fall. As the RBI chapter explains, every dollar it sells sucks rupees out of the banking system. Liquidity tightens. Overnight rates rise. And now the domestic boundary is under strain too: the government still needs to borrow its usual huge amount, banks have less spare cash to buy its bonds, and households have a thinner surplus to lend. Bond yields rise, and the squeeze spreads to companies and borrowers everywhere.

An oil shock is an external problem that becomes a domestic one through the RBI's reserves and the bond market.

That is why the same oil price can be a nuisance one year and a crisis the next. What matters is the condition of the balance sheet when the shock arrives: how wide the gap already is, how much of it rests on fast money, how much the government needs to borrow and how much spare saving households have. This cycle scores worse on two of those than the headline current account number suggests: households have a thinner surplus, and the funding mix leans on portfolio money.

history.title: The budget that could not be presented
history.story:
In early 1991 India was running out of dollars, and its government was running out of support. Prime Minister Chandra Shekhar led a minority government that survived on the Congress party's backing. Just before his finance minister, Yashwant Sinha, was due to present the annual budget, that backing collapsed. Sinha could only present a stopgap interim budget, and the government soon fell. Years later he said that, given the chance, he would have made much the same speech as his successor.

That successor was Manmohan Singh. In July 1991, with the rupee just devalued twice and reserves almost gone, he stood up to present a budget that cut the fiscal deficit and began dismantling the licence raj. He closed by paraphrasing Victor Hugo: no power on earth can stop an idea whose time has come.
history.lesson: The external account, not growth, is India's binding constraint, and a weak fiscal position makes it bind sooner.

history.title: Tying the government's hands by law
history.story:
After the 1991 scare, finance ministers kept promising to cut the deficit and kept missing. So in December 2000 Yashwant Sinha, now finance minister under Atal Bihari Vajpayee, introduced a bill that would write a deficit target into law. A watered-down version passed in 2003 as the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, with deficit targets due to be met by the end of the decade.

For a few years it worked. Then the global financial crisis hit and the targets were set aside. Sinha later grumbled that his successors had simply taken leave of the Act.
history.lesson: Fiscal rules are credible until the first big shock tests them, so watch the glide path, not the law.

history.title: Stimulus now, inflation later
history.story:
The deficit was already widening before the crisis. In early 2008 P. Chidambaram announced a giant farm loan waiver ahead of a general election, and government salaries were raised under a new pay commission. Then Lehman Brothers collapsed that September and the government cut taxes and raised spending to keep growth alive. Pranab Mukherjee, who took over the finance ministry, presented a budget in 2009 with the deficit sharply wider.

It worked in the short run: India bounced back faster than most. But a deficit that wide, meeting a drought and high food prices, fed the stubborn inflation of 2010 to 2013. Food inflation stayed in double digits for long stretches, and the RBI spent years trying to catch up.
history.lesson: Slippage can buy growth today, but the bill arrives later as inflation and higher rates.

history.title: The gold sermon
history.story:
By 2013 India's current account deficit had hit a record share of the economy, and gold imports were a big part of it. Chidambaram, back as finance minister, appealed to Indians to contain their passion for gold. Import duties were raised repeatedly, banks were told not to sell gold coins, and new rules tied gold imports to re-exports. Smuggling through airports and the Gulf took off.

Then the Fed hinted at slowing its bond buying, foreign money fled and the rupee crashed to a record low. India landed in Morgan Stanley's Fragile Five. A wide gap funded by hot money had met a shock from abroad.
history.lesson: A wide external gap funded by fast money is the most vulnerable configuration India can be in.

history.title: The savings puzzle
history.story:
In September 2023 the RBI published data showing that households' net financial savings had fallen to a near five-decade low as a share of the economy. Critics read it as a sign of distress. Within days the finance ministry pushed back, arguing that households were not struggling but borrowing to buy homes and vehicles, shifting from financial to physical assets.

The RBI's deputy governor Michael Patra offered a third reading: people were drawing down the cash they had hoarded during lockdowns. All three explanations have some truth. Meanwhile, the same households were pouring record sums into SIPs.
history.lesson: Domestic equity flows can get stronger even as the household cushion behind them gets thinner, so watch both.

history.title: The decade-long wait for the index
history.story:
For years Indian officials lobbied global index providers to include Indian government bonds in their emerging market indices. The sticking points were capital controls, taxes and settlement rules. In 2020 the RBI created a class of government bonds that foreigners could buy without limits, designed precisely to qualify.

In September 2023 JP Morgan announced that Indian bonds would join its flagship emerging-market index from June 2024, phased in over ten months. Bloomberg followed with its own index from 2025. Billions of dollars of passive money started arriving on a schedule, regardless of anyone's view on India.
history.lesson: Index money is fast in and can be fast out, so it funds the gap cheaply but does not make it safer.

today:
The balance sheet is being tested right now. Over the last twenty sessions, domestic institutions have bought a net [[val:dii20]] of Indian shares while foreign investors sold [[val:fii20]]. That is the household shift to markets doing its job.

The external side is under strain. Oil at [[val:brent]] a barrel, up [[val:brent_3m]] in three months, is widening the gap. The rupee at [[val:usdinr]] has stayed close to its weakest reading of [[val:usdinr_record]] only because the RBI is defending it. Reserves have been falling, and the RBI has raised the cash reserve requirement: the external defence is now draining domestic liquidity, exactly the boundary problem described above.

What to watch next: the quarterly current account data, monthly net direct investment, how much foreign money leaves the index-eligible bonds, and the size of the government's borrowing calendar for the second half of the year.
sowhat:
Thin household net savings and weak direct investment mean the external gap is funded by the most volatile money. That is why an oil shock bites harder this cycle than the headline current account number suggests.

  • Prefer lenders with a large base of cheap, sticky retail deposits. When liquidity tightens and savings are scarce, a stable deposit base is the most valuable asset in finance.
  • Be careful with lenders that grew fast on unsecured consumer credit and those that fund themselves in the bond market. Thin household cushions and tight liquidity hit both.
  • Be careful with companies carrying large unhedged dollar loans. A weaker rupee raises their debt overnight.
  • Gold-linked businesses, such as gold loan companies, tend to benefit when rupee gold prices rise, though jewellery demand can soften at very high prices.

What would flip it: oil falling back would narrow the gap, a pick-up in net direct investment would make its funding stickier, and a recovery in household net savings would loosen the domestic boundary. Any two of those together would make Indian assets far less fragile to the next shock.
